acts.title: The Stain Is the Proof — Copyist's Quarter
acts.desc: Lisbon Copyist's Quarter. Afonso the copyist explains the authentication chain for a water-stained quire in Camões's own hand — pages 12–17 bear a crystallized tideline at the exact height the sea reached the night he swam ashore holding the manuscript above his head. Insight DC 12: understand the specific phrase — 'the salt on the binding' — that only Father Bento's memory of the original dedication letter can confirm.
acts.passText: You hear the specific phrase before he says it. You move for MDN immediately.
acts.failText: Afonso explains the phrase. You understand. The quire is in your hands.

acts.title: The Stain Is the Proof — Mountain Road
acts.desc: Mountain road to Father Bento's villa. A Venetian buyer's agent intercepts and demands the quire for 'independent transport.' Persuasion DC 13: breaking chain of custody destroys the authentication value he claims to protect — without Bento's memory of the original dedication letter confirmed in sequence, the tideline cannot be authenticated.
acts.passText: He understands the argument. He turns back.
acts.failText: He argues further. You name the specific authentication gap his intervention would create. He steps aside, dissatisfied.

acts.title: The Stain Is the Proof — Prior's Rule
acts.desc: Mountain monastery. Bento's dedication letter has been mistakenly sent to the scriptorium; the prior will not release documents without the abbot's seal. Persuasion DC 14: the rule does not apply to property received in error — the letter is not the monastery's document. Combat 2× monastery porters AC 12 HP 16 if failed.
acts.passText: The prior reads the argument. He releases the letter.
acts.failText: Combat: two porters, AC 12, HP 16. The letter is released afterward — they were defending procedure, not the document.

acts.title: The Stain Is the Proof — Mudslide
acts.desc: Mountain road back to the city — partially blocked by mudslide. Alternate path is passable but slow. Athletics DC 13: reach the notary before vespers.
acts.passText: The alternate path opens on a clear ridge. You reach the notary with an hour to spare.
acts.failText: The path is slower than expected. You arrive at vespers. The notary is still at his desk — barely.

acts.title: The Stain Is the Proof — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. The notary has closed the intake register for the day. His assistant Luca recognizes the quire. Insight DC 12: the reframing that gives Caspar professional cover — re-registration of prior property, not a new submission.
acts.passText: Caspar finds the category in his own register. He reopens it without breaking his rule. The quire is accessioned.
acts.failText: Caspar finds the category himself, slowly. It takes twenty minutes. The quire is accessioned.

acts.title: What the Cape Already Knew — Melinda Study
acts.desc: Melinda, East Africa. Ahmed ibn Yusuf's manuscript — a bound record of African traditional knowledge of the Cape spirit, predating the Portuguese fleet's first passage. Frei António gives you the manuscript and explains: a Tangier agent has been in the trading district for three weeks. WIS DC 12: the agent is following the manuscript, not the friar.
acts.passText: You watch before leaving. The agent moves when you do.
acts.failText: You carry the manuscript without noting the agent. He follows from a distance you do not see.

acts.title: What the Cape Already Knew — Harbor Inspection
acts.desc: Lisbon harbor. A Portuguese harbor official — Sebastião — wants to log the manuscript's subject entry before it leaves the port. He is considering 'indigenous spirit tradition — maritime implications.' Persuasion DC 12: it is cultural correspondence, not intelligence — 'cultural correspondence, traditional coastal knowledge, Melinda court series.'
acts.passText: You say: 'Cultural correspondence — traditional coastal knowledge, Melinda court series.' Sebastião writes it. He closes the ledger without asking again.
acts.failText: Sebastião writes 'indigenous spirit tradition — maritime implications.' The maritime court will have that entry before the ship reaches Lisbon. The document still leaves.

acts.title: What the Cape Already Knew — Ship Factor
acts.desc: On the ship. The factor Luís presses about the package's contents — he will mention it to a colleague at the Lisbon dock if not satisfied, creating a gap in the chain of custody. Persuasion DC 13: describe Ahmed's work as what it preserves, not what it claims.
acts.passText: You describe Ahmed's work in terms of what it preserves rather than what it claims. Luís nods. 'His geographical work is remarkable.' He goes back to his cabin.
acts.failText: Luís is satisfied with enough to close the conversation, but he will mention it to a colleague at the Lisbon dock. That mention becomes a gap in the chain of custody.

acts.title: What the Cape Already Knew — Maritime Officials
acts.desc: Lisbon harbor arrival. Maritime court officials board looking for the manuscript. Combat 2× officials AC 12 HP 18 if they invoke detention provisions — the seal must remain intact as the only evidence the chain of custody was never broken.
acts.passText: Both officials are down. The seal is intact. You reach Lisbon at first light.
acts.failText: They invoke a maritime compact provision. The manuscript is held overnight. You are present at the release the following morning — they found no grounds to seize. One day lost.

acts.title: What the Cape Already Knew — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Frei Tomás at the humanist intake desk. The archive receives Ahmed ibn Yusuf's manuscript — the African traditional knowledge of the Cape spirit, predating the Portuguese fleet. WIS DC 11: name each hand the manuscript passed through from Ahmed's study to this desk.
acts.passText: You name each hand. Frei Tomás writes it all. He takes the manuscript. 'Ahmed ibn Yusuf's name goes in the compiler's column. Not the fleet's.'
acts.failText: Frei Tomás notes a gap in the chain. He enters the document with a caveat: 'chain of custody unverified at one point.' But the document is in the archive's custody.

acts.title: The Restelo Dissent — Dying Monk
acts.desc: Mountain monastery, Sintra Hills. Dying Brother Sebastião wants the quire of the Old Man of Restelo's complete speech — written by one private monk, held for forty-five years, never in any official chronicle — filed at the royal chronicle commission. WIS DC 11: the commission would file it as an appendix subordinated to the official account; the humanist archive preserves it independently.
acts.passText: You redirect. You explain the distinction. Brother Sebastião closes his eyes. 'Yes,' he says. 'That is correct.'
acts.failText: You carry the quire toward the chronicle commission. Brother Sebastião does not disagree; he has thought about it differently and cannot explain why.

acts.title: The Restelo Dissent — Royal Herald
acts.desc: Monastery gate. A royal herald has an order for 'documents of historical interest' from the monastery. Persuasion DC 12: a private monk's private copy of a private citizen's speech is not a crown document — it is intellectual property of the monk's estate, designated by his authorization to the humanist archive.
acts.passText: The herald reads the argument. He notes in his register: 'item declined — private estate property, not crown documentation.' He steps aside.
acts.failText: The herald accepts a temporary receipt and notes the quire in the crown register as 'item pending confirmation of private-estate status.' You have forty-eight hours before the status is confirmed against you.

acts.title: The Restelo Dissent — Chronicle Commission
acts.desc: Lisbon, approach to the archive. A chronicle commission official offers appendix filing — broad visibility but subordinated to the official account's toleration of the dissent. WIS DC 12: an appendix changes the document from dissent itself into a qualification of the official account.
acts.passText: He accepts the distinction. He says he will commission a separate notation in the chronicle referencing the humanist archive's holding. You tell him that would be exactly right.
acts.failText: He follows you to the archive and speaks with Frei Tomás. Frei Tomás decides for independent filing, but the delay costs two hours.

acts.title: The Restelo Dissent — River Ford
acts.desc: Flooded river ford — twenty pages of Brother Sebastião's handwriting, ink cannot get wet. Athletics DC 11: steady crossing, dry route.
acts.passText: You ford cleanly. The quire is dry. The marginal note is intact.
acts.failText: You slip at the center. The quire's bottom edge catches a splash — the final page takes a small water stain. The ink is safe. But the corner of Brother Sebastião's marginal note is blurred.

acts.title: The Restelo Dissent — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads the speech. Investigation DC 11: confirm no existing category covers public speech at an official gathering officially not admitted — not suppressed, simply not recorded.
acts.passText: Sweelinck creates: 'Dissent Records — Public Protest Made in Full View and Then Allowed Not to Exist, First Entry. The Old Man of Restelo's speech: made publicly, heard by thousands, written by one private monk, held for forty-five years; the absence was not an act of state but of omission.'
acts.failText: Filed under Unofficial Accounts — Unverified Testimonials. The speech is in the archive but under a category that implies it might not be accurate.

acts.title: Inês de Castro's Testimony — Estate Sale
acts.desc: Lisbon Copyist's Quarter. A notary's estate is being settled — the executor is selling historical materials as curiosities. A folded parchment marked 'Portugal, 14th century, marriage documentation, royal adjacent.' History DC 11: three men were ordered to execute Inês de Castro; if Pedro's marriage to her was legally valid, their act was regicide, not execution. The executor does not know what he is selling.
acts.passText: You explain the legal weight to the executor. He raises the price. You pay the raised price.
acts.failText: You buy it at the curiosity price without explaining why it matters. The executor asks if you want anything else from the box.

acts.title: Inês de Castro's Testimony — The Loyalists
acts.desc: CVP street. Two men watching the estate. They follow you. One speaks: he represents interests that preferred a particular reading of the 14th century. Persuasion DC 12: destroying it doesn't erase the marriage — it leaves the classification permanently uncertain; a definitive answer either way is more useful to posterity than sustained ambiguity.
acts.passText: One of them says: 'You're going to the archive anyway.' He says it as a prediction, not a question. He steps aside.
acts.failText: They offer to buy the document instead. You decline. They follow at a distance until the city gate.

acts.title: Inês de Castro's Testimony — Canon Law Scholar
acts.desc: Rome, Vatican archive approach. A canon law scholar wants a brief loan of the attestation for an active Curia precedent case. Insight DC 12: active use in one proceeding consumes its primary evidential status; filed at a neutral archive it is available to any future case including ones not yet foreseeable.
acts.passText: He accepts the reasoning. He asks for a reference to the archive entry once it is filed so he can cite it as a secondary source.
acts.failText: He follows you into the archive vestibule arguing the urgency. The archivist has to manage the entry.

acts.title: Inês de Castro's Testimony — Alpine Steps
acts.desc: Alpine pass north of Rome — frozen stone footbridge, twelve glazed steps, guide rope, ten-foot footbridge over a frozen trickle. The parchment must arrive dry and unfolded. Athletics DC 11: weight on the guide rope, heels down, hands steady.
acts.passText: You descend carefully, weight on the rope, and cross the footbridge without incident.
acts.failText: Your boot slides on the third step. You catch the rope with both hands. The pack holds. You retrieve it and continue down.

acts.title: Inês de Castro's Testimony — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads the attestation. He reads the reverse line: 'Quod Deus conjunxit.' 'Someone knew this might matter.' Perception DC 11: verify the three witness signatures and notary stamp are in the same ink age as the date notation — not added afterward.
acts.passText: You confirm the contemporaneous dating. Sweelinck writes: 'Retroactive Legal Classification Records — The Document That Changes the Definition of a Crime Already Committed, First Entry.' The reverse notation is filed as part of the document and not separated.
acts.failText: Sweelinck notes the ink assessment as provisional — 'not independently verified.' The attestation enters the archive with a provenance caveat.

acts.title: Pacheco's Account — Historian's Priority
acts.desc: Lisbon Humanist Archive. Historian Fernão has the sealed folio — three months of Pacheco's dictated sessions, ending with his thumb-mark because his writing hand won't close properly. Fernão wants to file through the royal chronicle commission first. Insight DC 11: the commission that abandoned Pacheco would hold editorial authority over the testimony's access.
acts.passText: Fernão hears the argument. He is quiet. He looks at the folio. 'Duarte,' he says, quietly. He hands it over.
acts.failText: Fernão insists on the commission first. He lets you carry it to the archive as a second filing — which means the commission's version becomes the primary record.

acts.title: Pacheco's Account — Crown Secretary
acts.desc: LHA gate. A crown secretary wants review before archival deposit. His authorization covers standard testimonies. Persuasion DC 12: sealed by the deponent's explicit condition — breaking the seal voids the commission's terms; his authorization cannot cover testimonies with sealed-by-deponent conditions.
acts.passText: He reads the cover instruction. He reads it again. He steps back. He notes the commission condition in his record and does not further obstruct.
acts.failText: He files a formal review request to be processed after archival intake. The testimony enters the archive but with a crown review notation pending.

acts.title: Pacheco's Account — Venetian Consortium
acts.desc: Venice archive district. A Venetian merchant consortium factor wants to acquire Pacheco's testimony for a trade claim against the Portuguese crown. Insight DC 12: private acquisition makes it one party's instrument; filed at a neutral archive it is available to any proceeding including theirs.
acts.passText: He accepts the archive-access framing. He notes the Weimar entry category so his solicitors can cite it as a secondary source.
acts.failText: He follows you to the harbor and makes a second offer. You reach the ship before he has finished making it.

acts.title: Pacheco's Account — Wax Seal Night
acts.desc: Wet weather north of the Alps — a wayside hostel, the only heat from a fireplace. The wax seal cannot soften. Athletics DC 11: sleep in the cold corner of the hostel with the sealed folio between you and the wall.
acts.passText: You sleep cold. The seal is sharp and unaffected in the morning.
acts.failText: The seal softens slightly overnight. It rehardened in a different impression — the eagle-device is now partially obscured. Sweelinck will note it as a minor provenance deviation.

acts.title: Pacheco's Account — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck breaks the seal according to Pacheco's instruction — this is the designated unsealing location. He reads forty minutes of session sheets. The thumb-marks. He says: 'Seven engagements. A hundred men. Seven assembled armies. Then an almshouse.' Investigation DC 11: a category that names the gap between commission performed and recognition never paid.
acts.passText: Sweelinck creates: 'Abandoned Hero Records — The Commission Performed in Full and Never Paid in the Currency the Kingdom Owes, First Entry. The thumb-marks at the end of each session are the record of a man who could not hold a stylus.'
acts.failText: Filed under Distinguished Military Records — Testimonies. Pacheco's account is in the archive, but the abandonment is not named in the category.

acts.title: Monsaide's Letter — Friar's Problem
acts.desc: Melinda Scholar's Court. Frei António gives you the codex — Monsaide's three-session letter in Arabic with Latin translation, knotted circles at each session end. A Tangier agent has been in the Melinda trading district for three weeks and has not approached the friar directly. Insight DC 11: the agent is following the codex, not the friar — watch before leaving.
acts.passText: You watch before leaving. The agent moves when you do. He is following the codex.
acts.failText: You carry the codex without noting the agent. He follows from a distance you do not see.

acts.title: Monsaide's Letter — Tangier Claim
acts.desc: Melinda harbor. The Tangier agent intercepts. He claims the letter names family business arrangements — private commercial information. Persuasion DC 12: the business arrangements are context for Monsaide's moral decision, not its subject; a conscience-letter is not suppressed by commercial privacy interests in its contextual details.
acts.passText: He accepts the conscience-versus-commerce distinction. He notes that if the archive files under Monsaide's name, the commercial context will be discoverable in full. You say yes, that is true. He says nothing further.
acts.failText: The agent files a legal claim with the Melinda trading post factor. The claim will follow the codex to wherever it is filed.

acts.title: Monsaide's Letter — Trade Intelligence Flag
acts.desc: Constantinople trade administration. A Byzantine official wants to classify the codex under commercial intelligence — the named Moorish merchants have ongoing arrangements in his district. Insight DC 12: commercial names embedded in a moral testimony are context; classifying under trade records permanently misclassifies the letter's subject.
acts.passText: He accepts that commercial names embedded in a moral testimony are context, not intelligence. He lifts the flag.
acts.failText: He flags the codex for commercial intelligence review — a two-week hold. It reaches Weimar with a notation: 'commercial content under review.'

acts.title: Monsaide's Letter — River Ferry
acts.desc: River crossing north of Constantinople, slow ferry, tight ship connection — the codex cannot cross by any route involving wading. Athletics DC 11: hold the right pace, know the exact path from the landing to the port.
acts.passText: You have the port road clear in your head. You make the ship with twenty-five minutes to spare.
acts.failText: A cart blocks the port road for fifteen minutes. You arrive at the ship with seven minutes to spare.

acts.title: Monsaide's Letter — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads all three sessions. He says: 'He did not convert. He did not change sides. He made a specific calculation about what his assistance would prevent.' Investigation DC 11: no category covers the act that was neither conversion nor treason but a named moral calculation.
acts.passText: Sweelinck creates: 'Moral Calculation Records — The Act Across the Line That Was Neither Conversion Nor Betrayal, First Entry. The archive names this as a conscience and not as a side-change, because those are different things.'
acts.failText: Filed under Cross-Community Testimonies — Ambiguous Allegiance. The word 'ambiguous' misclassifies the act.

acts.title: The Adamastor Prophecy — Holding Order
acts.desc: Lisbon Humanist Archive. Survivor Carlos Ferreira has the sealed deposition but a maritime holding order prevents filing — 'evidence pending hearing' for an inquiry the commission will never actually conduct. Persuasion DC 12: a holding order for a proceeding that will never occur is void on its own terms.
acts.passText: The intake clerk reads the holding order's language carefully. He accepts the argument. The entry is filed without complication.
acts.failText: The archive intake clerk is uncertain. He accepts the deposition but notes the holding order as a pending complication.

acts.title: The Adamastor Prophecy — Commission Authority
acts.desc: LHA gate. A maritime court official reads the holding order as covering all documentation from the Cape inquiry — an expansion beyond the order's actual language. Insight DC 12: his expanded reading would need a separate order; he does not yet have it and cannot act on what he does not have.
acts.passText: You cite the difference between the order's language and his interpretation. He acknowledges the textual limitation. He says he will apply for an expanded order. He does not yet have it.
acts.failText: He files an amended holding order with the archive. Frei Tomás puts the deposition in a holding category for two weeks.

acts.title: The Adamastor Prophecy — Empire's Inconvenience
acts.desc: Constantinople Portuguese trade office. A trade representative wants the deposition routed through the royal archive for controlled access — it documents that Adamastor's prophecy was accurate. Persuasion DC 12: the archive does not adjudicate the prophecy's accuracy; routing to a controlled archive is directing suppression through institutional channels.
acts.passText: He accepts the archive's neutrality argument. He notes he will request access through proper scholarly channels.
acts.failText: He files a formal objection with the archive. Sweelinck will receive it alongside the deposition and will need to address it in his intake note.

acts.title: The Adamastor Prophecy — Shale Descent
acts.desc: Mountain terrain north of Constantinople — forty feet of loose shale on the path's steep left descent. The sealed parchment deposition cannot be cracked against stone. Athletics DC 12: controlled steps, back flat against the hill if needed, pack held against the body.
acts.passText: You descend carefully, weight back, feet testing each shale plate. The descent takes eight minutes. The pack arrives undamaged.
acts.failText: Your left foot skids three steps before you catch the rock face. The pack stays on. The seal is intact. Your hand is scraped.

acts.title: The Adamastor Prophecy — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads the deposition and finds a hairline repair at the fold edge — the wax was opened and re-pressed. Perception DC 11: the re-pressing is shallow, consistent with a brief opening at the maritime court's office before the wax cooled.
acts.passText: You tell Sweelinck: the re-pressing happened before the wax cooled — at the court's office when the holding order was issued. He creates: 'Prophecy Fulfillment Records — The Sworn Account Whose Three Words Named What Should Not Be Named, First Entry.' questComplete.
acts.failText: You cannot determine when it happened. Sweelinck notes 'seal condition uncertain — possible prior opening' in the provenance record.

acts.title: The Commission Letter — Chancery Secretary
acts.desc: Lisbon Humanist Archive. Frei Domingos, secretary to the crown's archival commission, has his hand on the commission letter's case — Dom Manuel's 1497 authorization to Gama, seal intact. He says it is a state instrument. Persuasion DC 12: the letter's operative life ended when Gama returned; what survives is testimony, not policy.
acts.passText: Frei Domingos folds the classification form. 'The letter is evidence,' he says, as if testing the word. He withdraws. The case is yours.
acts.failText: Frei Domingos notes your argument and files the classification form, allowing the archive to contest it. The letter stays, under dispute.

acts.title: The Commission Letter — Duplicate Copy
acts.desc: Cape Verde waypoint. A Lisbon merchant factor named Esteves has a notarial copy of the commission letter from the court's retained exemplar. He wants to trade: the copy for the original. Insight DC 13: determine whether Esteves knows the difference, or whether he is acting for someone who does and who prefers the original to disappear into a private collection.
acts.passText: Esteves knows exactly what he is offering — acting for a Venetian collector who understands the original's singular provenance. He will not stop you, but has confirmed: the archive needs to know this when it accessions.
acts.failText: Esteves is opaque. You decline the trade but leave uncertain. A note under your cabin door that night: 'The duplicate is already in Venice. Think about what that means.'

acts.title: The Commission Letter — Zamorim's Question
acts.desc: Malindi. Swahili scholar Bwana Fahari will not certify the provenance chain until the exchange's nature is resolved: was Gama's presentation of the letter a diplomatic presentation or a display of force? History DC 13: it was a presentation — the Zamorim handed it back because he could not read it and had interpreters for that purpose.
acts.passText: Fahari nods slowly. 'It was a presentation,' he says. 'Like any letter of introduction. The refusal came later, from different men, for different reasons.' He certifies the provenance chain.
acts.failText: Fahari declines to certify. He will write a note of contested provenance — 'function unclear, possibly coercive instrument' — that will follow the letter.

acts.title: The Commission Letter — Mountain Road
acts.desc: Road north from Constantinople. A Venetian courier overtakes you — his saddle bags are wrong for dispatches, he arrived from the wrong direction, and he has been matching your pace for an hour. He will attempt to take the satchel by force if you show uncertainty. Athletics DC 14: physical readiness that does not escalate but does not yield.
acts.passText: He reads your posture correctly and decides the risk is wrong. He nods, touches his hat, and rides ahead. The commission letter arrives intact.
acts.failText: He gets a hand on the satchel strap. The strap tears. He has the outer sleeve — empty. The commission letter is still under your coat, wrapped in oilcloth.

acts.title: The Commission Letter — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads the commission letter for forty minutes. 'The king who wrote this has been dead for seventy years. What does the archive do with a document whose authorization has outrun its author by a century?' Investigation DC 13: the commission letter is a historical act; the archive classifies by what the document did, not by what it might be taken to justify.
acts.passText: Sweelinck says: 'A departure. Yes. The archive can classify a departure.' He writes: 'Royal Commission Records — The Letter That Authorized the Opening of the Eastern World, First Entry. The consequences belong to history; the document belongs here.'
acts.failText: Sweelinck writes: 'Authorization instrument — scope disputed.' The letter is filed under administrative documents pending a second review.

acts.title: The False Pilot's Chart — Merchant's Grandson
acts.desc: East African waypoint. Habib, grandson of the merchant whose house received the False Pilot's Chart as scrap packing from a fleet transaction, wants a written statement clearing his family before the chart becomes evidence of a conspiracy that touched them only accidentally. Persuasion DC 12: the archive records provenance accurately — received in good faith as scrap packing — not advocacy.
acts.passText: Habib accepts the distinction. 'The truth is enough,' he says, quietly. 'My grandfather would have wanted it known.' You receive the False Pilot's Chart.
acts.failText: Habib is not satisfied. He will give you the chart but asks that you note his request at the archive. He will write a separate letter to Sweelinck. The chart comes with a dispute attached.

acts.title: The False Pilot's Chart — Regent's Descendant
acts.desc: Still at the East African waypoint. A descendant of the Mozambique regent wants the chart destroyed — the two separate false notations in two hands prove premeditated coordination, not mere incompetence. Insight DC 12: the descendant is here because the chart reaching an archive is more damaging than disappearing — read his actual level of risk tolerance.
acts.passText: He is frightened, not threatening. You tell him: the archive classifies evidence, not judgment. He stands in the sun for a moment, then walks away without speaking.
acts.failText: You cannot fully read him. You hold the chart and board the ship. At your next port, a message is waiting: someone asks that you reconsider.

acts.title: The False Pilot's Chart — Navigation Scholar
acts.desc: Constantinople Ottoman chart library. Cartographer Mehmed Çelebi has authenticated the chart — accurate in every detail except the false channel. Investigation DC 12: work through his methodology to confirm the single altered element and establish that the rest of the chart's accuracy makes the falsification undeniable.
acts.passText: Çelebi points to the channel notation: 'The soundings around it are exact. The pilot knew the depth at every point. He chose this one spot to draw the channel into the reef. No one who drew the rest of this chart could have made that error by accident.'
acts.failText: Çelebi is uncertain about one secondary notation. His authentication note reads: 'possibly deliberate, inconclusive.' The chart's evidential value is reduced.

acts.title: The False Pilot's Chart — Danube Crossing
acts.desc: Danube crossing, early spring, flat-bottomed barge. Halfway across, the current catches the stern — the barge swings broadside. The chart in its leather case is under your arm. The ink on coastal leather does not survive submersion. Athletics DC 13: cross the deck, get a hand on the stern rail, give the working ferryman stability to bring the bow around.
acts.passText: You cross the deck in four steps, hit the stern rail, and brace. The ferryman gets the pole set. You arrive on the north bank dry. The chart is intact.
acts.failText: You keep the chart dry but go to one knee on the wet deck. The case skids two feet before you catch it. The ferryman corrects the barge unassisted.

acts.title: The False Pilot's Chart — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck holds the chart at arm's length under the north light. 'What do I call this? It is not a diplomatic document. It is not a literary text. It is a physical instrument of attempted murder that happened to fail.' Investigation DC 12: propose the classification — navigational record with forensic annotation; charts belong to cartographic collections.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Cartographic Records — The Chart Drawn to Kill: A Coastal Navigation Document with a Surgical Falsification, First Entry. Accurate in every detail but one; the one detail is a reef where the chart draws a channel; the fleet it was meant to destroy arrived in India anyway.'
acts.failText: Filed under 'uncategorized instruments of the Indian voyage.' It will be reclassified eventually.

acts.title: The Zamorim's Diplomatic Record — Scribe's Descendant
acts.desc: Malindi. Merchant Rajan has the Zamorim's Court Register Entry — a palm-leaf folio in Malayalam recording the 1498 Gama audience from the Indian side. Three buyers: you, a Portuguese crown representative (Frei Simão, says it belongs to Portugal), and a Venetian factor (private collection). Persuasion DC 13: the folio is the Zamorim's document — it cannot belong to Portugal because it is not Portugal's.
acts.passText: Rajan considers for a long moment. 'The archive,' he says. 'Because the Zamorim would have wanted it read.' He hands you the tin box.
acts.failText: Frei Simão outbids you financially. The folio is held for Simão's review of the price. Rajan will speak with you again if you return with a counter-argument.

acts.title: The Zamorim's Diplomatic Record — Simão's Objection
acts.desc: Malindi dock. Frei Simão cites the law of discovery — Portugal's claim to the sea route extends to documents about that discovery. Insight DC 12: the law of discovery covers what was found; it does not cover the records kept by the people who were already there.
acts.passText: The weakness is clear: the Zamorim was not discovered; he was visited. His scribe's entry is his own record of a visitor. Simão opens his mouth, closes it. He steps aside.
acts.failText: Simão is not wrong enough to dismiss cleanly. He files a formal objection. A hold order will reach the next port ahead of you.

acts.title: The Zamorim's Diplomatic Record — Translation Problem
acts.desc: Constantinople. Greek scholar Nikolaos has translated the folio. The final phrase can mean 'watched carefully' or 'understood carefully.' Investigation DC 12: the surrounding context supports cautious inquiry — polite refusal, genuine deliberation — not hostile surveillance.
acts.passText: Nikolaos reviews the full entry. 'Understood carefully,' he says. 'The Zamorim wanted to understand these men before deciding what to do with them.' The translation is unambiguous.
acts.failText: Nikolaos marks both readings in the translation. The archive will receive a document with an unresolved ambiguity in its central interpretive line.

acts.title: The Zamorim's Diplomatic Record — Courier Road
acts.desc: North of Constantinople. A fellow traveler named Petar asks too many questions about your destination — not what is in the box but where you are going with it. Perception DC 13: identify the tell — his left hand rests on his belt in the exact position of a man accustomed to carrying a concealed weapon.
acts.passText: His left hand rests on his belt in the exact position. No sword, no knife visible — but the resting position is trained. You change your route at the next crossroads and lose him in an hour.
acts.failText: Petar's tell is subtle enough that you cannot be certain. A horse outside the next waystation has been ridden hard from the south.

acts.title: The Zamorim's Diplomatic Record — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck says: 'The Zamorim watched them carefully and was right to. The Portuguese came back in 1502 and bombarded Calicut.' Investigation DC 12: propose the exact accession language — the receiving nation's account, belonging to the Gama collection but as a distinct voice.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Indian Ocean Diplomatic Records — The Receiving Nation's Account, First Entry. The final line reads: understood carefully. Four years later the Portuguese bombarded Calicut. This document belongs to the archive as the record of what the Zamorim thought before that happened.'
acts.failText: Filed under 'Eastern accounts of the Indian voyage.' A note reads: 'translation contested, final line ambiguous.'

acts.title: Venus's Island Account — Flemish Heir
acts.desc: Lisbon Humanist Archive. Flemish merchant Van Houten has a Dominican friar reviewing the Flemish Secretary's Interview Notes — Van der Berg's 1499 interview with three sailors describing the Island of Venus. Van Houten believes it requires Church judgment. Persuasion DC 12: separate the theological question from the archival one; the archive holds testimony, the Church holds judgment — different offices.
acts.passText: The Dominican reads your distinction aloud. Then: 'The archive holds testimony. The Church holds judgment. These are different offices.' He closes his breviary. Van Houten yields.
acts.failText: The Dominican wants to review the notes for three days. He releases them with a note: 'Contents spiritually ambiguous. Not recommended for general circulation.'

acts.title: Venus's Island Account — Third Sailor's Son
acts.desc: Cape Verde. Manuel, son of the third sailor who would not describe his experience, wants a supplementary note: his father's silence should be read as a chosen statement of sufficiency, not an inability to describe. Insight DC 12: assess whether the supplementary note serves archival accuracy or serves Manuel's desire to rehabilitate a silence.
acts.passText: The note is accurate and the motive is irrelevant to its accuracy. You write: 'the silence was a chosen statement of sufficiency, not an indication of inability to describe. The subject said: that's enough. This should be read as testimony, not as refusal.'
acts.failText: Both are true simultaneously. The supplementary note is added, but with a hedged formulation: 'silence interpreted by the subject's son as chosen, not compelled.'

acts.title: Venus's Island Account — Allegorical Reading
acts.desc: Malindi. Jesuit Padre Henrique wants to classify the interview notes as allegorical illustration of the Lusiad. Investigation DC 12: Van der Berg interviewed the sailors in 1499; the Lusiad appeared in 1572. The sailors were not enacting the poem's allegory — the poem was later written partly from accounts like this one.
acts.passText: Padre Henrique goes very still. 'Seventy years,' he says. 'I had the dates wrong.' He withdraws the classification note. 'Then the poem is what Camões made of what they said.' The notes are reclassified as primary testimony.
acts.failText: Padre Henrique is unconvinced — he argues the allegory and the testimony are the same event viewed from different angles. His classification note is added as an alternative reading.

acts.title: Venus's Island Account — Night Road
acts.desc: Outside Constantinople, the road north, after dark. Two men step from the treeline with cudgels — this is a robbery, not an assassination. The notes are in the pack. Athletics DC 14: two cudgels at close range in the dark, without drawing a weapon.
acts.passText: You step into the space between them before either can wind up. Close work, bad range for cudgels. They recalculate and step back. You walk north at the same pace. They do not follow.
acts.failText: You take a blow across your left forearm deflecting a swing. You get enough distance to run. The pack stays on. The notes are intact but the ink of the second page has smeared slightly.

acts.title: Venus's Island Account — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads all six pages including the supplementary note. He says: 'Three sailors. All remember the same things. One cannot describe the woman. One chose silence because the experience was sufficient. And the Flemish secretary did not know what to make of any of it.' Investigation DC 11: a classification that does not foreclose the question of what the sailors actually experienced.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Testimony of the Indian Voyage — Three Sailors on the Island of Love, First Entry. The archivist does not adjudicate; the poet made it allegory; the archive holds what was said before the allegory was written.'
acts.failText: Sweelinck writes: 'Sailor accounts, probable embellishment, possibly allegorical in origin.' The notes are filed under literary background material.

acts.title: The Gift Inventory — Archivist's Reclassification
acts.desc: Lisbon Humanist Archive. The fleet quartermaster's gift inventory (four scarlet mantles, six feathered hats, brass cups, sugar) is currently in maritime provisioning files. A crown official named Soares has filed a reclassification order to bury it there permanently. Investigation DC 12: the inventory is a diplomatic brief — it records what was offered to a foreign sovereign in an official capacity.
acts.passText: The cataloguer writes: 'document reclassified to diplomatic records per the argument that its subject is the content of a sovereign presentation, not fleet logistics.' Soares is overridden.
acts.failText: The cataloguer defers the decision for a week. The inventory remains in limbo but you can take it — the dispute will follow it.

acts.title: The Gift Inventory — Monsaide's Market Valuations
acts.desc: Cape Verde. Scholar Ibrahim believes the secondary marginal valuations are in Monsaide's handwriting and wants to add a certification claiming Monsaide chose silence about the gifts' inadequacy. Insight DC 13: the handwriting certification and the inference about Monsaide's intent should be separated in the archive's notes.
acts.passText: Ibrahim accepts the separation. Certification: 'Secondary annotations consistent with Monsaide's hand.' Interpretation: 'Historian's inference — not archival determination.' The two claims are listed distinctly.
acts.failText: Ibrahim adds both the handwriting certification and the interpretation as a combined note. Future readers will have difficulty separating the certified fact from the interpretive inference.

acts.title: The Gift Inventory — Zamorim's Contempt
acts.desc: Malindi. Swahili historian Fatuma wants to classify the inventory as documentation of a diplomatic failure and add that the 1502 bombardment was the unresolved consequence. Persuasion DC 12: the protocol reading of the silent reception is archival fact; the 1502 connection is historical interpretation and should be attributed to her.
acts.passText: Fatuma considers. 'The protocol is fact. The bombardment consequence is my argument.' The archive receives both, correctly labelled.
acts.failText: Fatuma insists both points be presented as historical fact. The note is added in dispute.

acts.title: The Gift Inventory — Rain on the Road
acts.desc: Road north of Constantinople, three days of rain. The pack goes under for three seconds at a flooded ford. The inventory — a single page of Portuguese — is in an oilskin pouch inside your pack. Survival DC 12: make the correct decisions about handling a possibly-wet period document in cold field conditions.
acts.passText: You do not open the oilskin in the rain. You carry it inside your coat for two hours to the waystation. At the waystation, by candlelight: dry throughout. The margin notations are intact.
acts.failText: You carry it closed. At the waystation you find the inventory lightly damp at one edge. The ink has not run, but the margin notations are slightly blurred.

acts.title: The Gift Inventory — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive. Sweelinck reads the inventory: four scarlet mantles, six feathered hats, brass cups, sugar. He says: 'No wonder it was filed as provisioning.' He says: 'I need to write an accession note for a document that proves the most famous diplomatic mission of the age was sent with gifts for a market stall. How do I write that without it sounding like mockery?' Investigation DC 12.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Diplomatic Records — The Gift Inventory at Calicut, First Entry. The Zamorim received them without comment, which in Malabar court protocol constituted a formal rejection. The archive holds this document as a record of the gap between the voyage's ambition and its diplomatic preparation; the gap is noted, not judged.'
acts.failText: Sweelinck writes a careful but slightly deflating note that will be read as understated mockery by anyone who knows the context.

acts.title: The Official Voyage Log — Coimbra Copy
acts.desc: Lisbon Humanist Archive. Lisbon antiquarian Rodrigues claims the Coimbra copy of the voyage log is a 1820s nationalist forgery — his evidence is anachronistic phrasings. Investigation DC 13: his 'anachronisms' should be checked against the 1510 copy date, not 1498; if they are 1510 usages rather than 1820s usages, his forgery argument collapses.
acts.passText: All of Rodrigues's examples are consistent with sixteenth-century chancery Portuguese. His forgery argument collapses. The cataloguer releases the log.
acts.failText: Rodrigues has two examples that are genuinely difficult to date. The cataloguer places the log in contested status. You may take it but with a dispute annotation.

acts.title: The Official Voyage Log — Revised Entries
acts.desc: Cape Verde. Palaeographer Conceição needs a comparison sample to identify the hand of the two anomalous log entries. She has a candidate letter written by Gama in 1499, in the colonial records. Persuasion DC 12: get access to the comparison letter from the protective colonial archivist.
acts.passText: The archivist allows a supervised comparison. Conceição examines both hands for twenty minutes. 'The letterforms are consistent across six indicators.' The identification note: 'secondary insertions highly consistent with Vasco da Gama, 1499.'
acts.failText: The colonial archivist allows only visual inspection. Conceição works from photographs. 'Possibly consistent with Gama's hand, comparison inconclusive.'

acts.title: The Official Voyage Log — Casa da Índia Destruction
acts.desc: Malindi. Portuguese archivist Santos has found the 1510 copy order, which says 'copy to be kept at Coimbra as protection against loss of original.' Insight DC 12: assess whether the 1510 order language genuinely supports equal authority for the survival copy, or whether this is post-hoc rationalization.
acts.passText: The 1510 order language is explicit: 'the copy shall serve in all purposes as the original, should the original be unavailable.' Santos is correct. The note is added without qualification.
acts.failText: The 1510 copy order language is ambiguous on the question of equal authority. Santos adds his note with the caveat 'interpretation contested.'

acts.title: The Official Voyage Log — Final Road
acts.desc: Three days north of Constantinople. Portuguese naval officer Capitão Braga overtakes you, riding the same road. 'A friend of mine is very interested in what you are carrying.' He names no friend. Persuasion DC 14: decline in a way that is final, courteous, and leaves no room for a counter-offer.
acts.passText: Braga listens to your answer and rides in silence. Then: 'My friend will be disappointed.' He touches his hat and takes a fork in the road south. You arrive at Weimar the following evening without further contact.
acts.failText: Braga is not satisfied but is not hostile. He rides ahead. At the Weimar city gate, a man in a gray coat is waiting and notes your arrival time.

acts.title: The Official Voyage Log — Archive
acts.desc: Weimar archive, evening. Sweelinck reads the voyage log slowly. He reads the two anomalous entries twice. 'Gama wrote these himself. Into his own notary's log.' He says: 'The country appeared much greater than we supposed. We departed with less than we came for but with the knowledge that we had been there.' Investigation DC 12: propose the formulation that names all four layers and holds the Gama identification at its appropriate level of confidence.
acts.passText: Sweelinck writes: 'Indian Voyage Records — The Official Log of the São Gabriel, First Entry. A fourth hand, identified as highly consistent with Gama's own, inserted two entries in the Calicut section. These insertions are not administrative language; they are a man trying to say what happened to him in the only record he knew would survive. The archive holds the skeleton beneath the poem. The poem was written later. The skeleton was always here.' questComplete.
acts.failText: Sweelinck writes a careful accession note that slightly hedges the Gama identification in a way that will cause future readers to discount it.
